Implications of using written description
A written description uses natural language to express an algorithm.
Because of this it can be coded in many languages and would
therefore be suitable in this case as the final language to be used
has not been chosen yet.
It is also suitable for non-technical audiences as specific
programming language constructs are not used, so the developer
could explain the solution to the non-competent programmer.
 
However written descriptions are not executable meaning that
testing on a computer is not possible, and the algorithm must be
tested and evaluated by humans, which could take a long time and
be problematic.
Another drawback is that there are few tools to aid in the writing of
descriptions of algorithms and therefore errors such as undeclared
variables or writing past the end of files would not be highlighted.
Also there is no standard convention for the type of
language/instructions that can be used and this can be problematic
if people with different backgrounds need to use the algorithm.

Suitability Bubble Sort
• A relatively simple algorithm, that has a stopping condition to
exit the sort once all numbers are in order. However it is a slow
algorithm and will take a long time to perform as the file is
many millions of records long.
• It is therefore suitable for data that is partially in order,
however the file is currently in chronological order and is
unlikely to be in any order based on email addresses.
• It is an inplace sort and does not require any extra memory
allocation, however the size of the file is large and cannot all
be held in memory at once.
Suitability of a Merge Sort
• It is a complex algorithm, however many prebuilt modules to
perform the function are available.
• It is a very fast algorithm, as it uses the divide and
conquer/recursive approach and is well suited for very
large data sets, such as this file of millions of records.
• The growth factor is not large, meaning that any future sorts
will not take an unduly longer time.
• It is not an in place sort, and can use backing store to
temporarily store smaller lists, making it very suitable for this
situation, as the file is too large to fit into main memory
 
Conclusion 
The reward for the evaluative conclusion should be based on the
student’s own analysis and application of knowledge and
understanding. 
In concluding, a student should consider: 
1. The relative proportion / balance or imbalance of competing
points (e.g. for and against / pros and cons / advantages and
disadvantages)

points.

• The best option is to use a merge sort as it is very fast and
future sort speeds will not increase massively if the file size
grows.
• Also its memory requirements are lower than for the bubble

Do not accept responses that are not relevant/appropriate in this

Positive impact for the supermarket
It would save ongoing costs as the number of manned checkouts
could be reduced, saving on wage costs.
There would be an increase of four checkout systems and this would
allow greater throughput and reduce customer wait times.
Using self service checkouts can also allow for more customer privacy
as no human would be see the goods being bought. This could lead to
greater sales of certain items.
All cash payments are automated leading to a reduction in human error
due to staff miscounting change.
Staff can be redirected from checkouts to other tasks such as
stacking shelves or helping customers in other ways.
It would allow the supermarket to meet the needs of customers who
have social anxiety
 
Negative impact for the supermarket
There would be disruption as manual checkouts must be removed,
and the area prepared to accept the new machines.
New hardware must be bought and installed, and this would have a
high initial cost.
The checkouts cannot be totally unmanned as a member of staff is
needed to supervise the system and help customers.
Some customers do want to use these systems and if there are fewer
manual checkouts then there could be increases wait times at these
points.

but learners should be rewarded for other pertinent

Benefits
This is a simple backup system, with only two disks being used, one
for the weekly fullback and one for the nightly incremental backup.
In the event of data loss, it would allow a students work to be
recovered by using the previous full back and the incremental
backup.
The fullback up disk is kept off site so any disasters at the college
such as floods or fires would not affect the full backup.
The incremental backup would only copy files that have changed
and this is likely to be a fraction of all files therefore this backup
would not take too much time. This would also reduce storage
requirements.
 
Drawbacks
The full backup is only removed off site on Monday evening,
therefore if any disaster was to occur between Friday evening and
Monday evening then the only full back up could be lost.
The incremental back is only kept on site, and this is risky.
Additionally, only one generation of this backup is kept meaning
that a failure could result in a day’s work being lost.
Recovery from the disaster is a lot slower using an incremental
system as it requires the full backup to be merged with the
incremental backup.
 
Conclusion
The reward for the evaluative conclusion should be based on
the student's own analysis and application of knowledge and
understanding.
